content: The Alcohol Use Disorders Identification Test (AUDIT) is a screening tool designed to identify individuals with problematic alcohol consumption. The AUDIT-C, a shorter version of the AUDIT, consists of three questions and can be administered using paper-and-pencil or through an interviewer. It has demonstrated sensitivities ranging from 18% to 100% and specificities between 71% and 100%, depending on the population and cut-off points used. The CAGE questionnaire is another screening tool for alcohol use disorders, consisting of four questions. It is typically self-administered using paper-and-pencil and was not initially validated for use in prenatal or pregnant populations. Sensitivities for the CAGE range from 38% to 59%, while specificities are between 82% and 92%. The NET (Not Early Testing) alcohol screening tool includes three questions and is administered via paper-and-pencil. It has been used in both inpatient and outpatient settings, with sensitivities ranging from 24% to 71% and specificities between 86% and 99%. The Short Michigan Alcohol Screening Test (SMAST) is a 13-item questionnaire designed to screen for alcohol use disorders. It is self-administered using paper-and-pencil and has sensitivities ranging from 11% to 15% and specificities between 96% and 98%. The Ten Question Drinking History (TQDH) is a 10-item interviewer-administered tool used in prenatal clinics to assess alcohol consumption. It is specifically designed for use in pregnant populations. The T-ACE questionnaire is a four-item screening tool for alcohol use, administered via paper-and-pencil, and is commonly used in prenatal clinics. Sensitivities for the T-ACE range from 60% to 91%, while specificities are between 37% and 79%. The TWEAK screening tool consists of five questions and is also administered via paper-and-pencil. It is frequently used in prenatal clinics, with sensitivities ranging from 59% to 92% and specificities between 64% and 92%. It is important to note that the sensitivities and specificities of these tools vary depending on the cut-off points used to determine risk. Additionally, some tools were not initially developed or validated for use in pregnant populations, which may affect their applicability in this context. The harmful use of alcohol and illicit drugs is the third leading risk factor for premature deaths and disabilities worldwide. In 2004, approximately 5 million people globally died from alcohol-related causes, including 320,000 young individuals aged 15 to 29 years.
